title: Bhai Sangat Singh
hookLine: tradition says a Sikh who looked like the Guru wore his plume at Chamkaur so the Guru could slip away

cards: Night at Chamkaur. The mud-walled house is ringed by an army that will attack again at first light. Inside, only a handful of Sikhs are left.

They have told the Guru he must go, so the community will not lose him, and the Guru has agreed. But an army watches a house like this. If the Guru's tall plume disappears from the wall, they'll know.
Someone has to stay behind and be seen: someone who, in the dark and at a distance, could pass for him. Today: Bhai Sangat Singh.

teach.b: Tradition says Bhai Sangat Singh looked like Guru Gobind Singh, close enough in look and build that, from below, in poor light, he could be taken for him.
So before the Guru left, he gave Sangat Singh his own plume, the kalgi, a jeweled ornament worn on the turban, along with his garments.
Sangat Singh put them on and took the Guru's place in the house, where the enemy could see him. Then, in the dark, the Guru slipped out with a few companions.

When morning came, the army attacked again, believing the Guru was inside. Sangat Singh and the Sikhs with him fought until they fell. Tradition says the enemy at first thought they had killed the Guru himself.
It wasn't a trick for its own sake.
It was a gift of time. Every hour the soldiers spent watching the plume on the wall was an hour the Guru was further away.

teach.h: TAKING THE DANGER, NOT THE HONOR.
teach.b: Sangat Singh wasn't taking the Guru's honor. He was taking the Guru's danger.
Some tellings give part of this story to another Sikh, Bhai Sant Singh, and some speak of the two together.
The details shift between tellings, but the shape stays the same: a Sikh who put on what marked the Guru, and stood where the Guru would have stood, so the Guru could live.
Sikhs call his name with love, not for looking like the Guru, but for what he did with that likeness.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Sangat Singh in remembrances of Chamkaur, especially in December when the martyrdoms of that season are recalled, and the gurdwara at Chamkaur keeps the memory of those who fell there.

games.q: you're Sangat Singh. the Guru must escape tonight, and from a distance you could pass for him. he hands you his plume. what do you do?
o: go with the Guru to protect him on the road.
put on the plume and stay where the enemy can see you.
hide the plume so no one is a target.
games.why: tradition says he put on the kalgi and stayed in the Guru's place. in the morning the army attacked believing the Guru was inside, and he fell there.

practice: This isn't about lying for anyone; it's about stepping into a hard spot so someone else can get through.
Think of someone near you who's carrying too much right now, a coworker who's behind, a parent who hasn't had a night off, and ask what you could take on so they could step away for a while.
Let one thing come: a shift, a dinner, a phone call.

wordCard.voice: Sangat Singh. The Sikh who, tradition says, wore the Guru's plume at Chamkaur and stood in his place, so the Guru could get away. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kalgi, the plume worn on the turban; Guru Gobind Singh is sometimes called the one with the plume.

carryVoice: Your line: he took his place. He took the danger, not the honor. Until tomorrow.
